Chapter 2: Building a Business in a Closed Economy—Challenges and Surprises
Starting a business is always a leap of faith, right? But imagine doing it in North Korea. There, it’s not just a leap—it’s like stepping straight into the unknown. The rules? Totally different. The risks are higher, and if the rewards come at all, you really have to earn them.
For anyone coming in from the outside, the first big hurdle is simply figuring out how things actually work. Sure, there are official regulations. But just as important—maybe even more so—are the unwritten rules. You know, those subtle signals that tell you what’s truly possible, and what’s completely off limits.
The journey usually kicks off with meeting after meeting. You’ll sit down with government officials, factory managers, local partners—the list goes on. Every decision is up for negotiation, and patience isn’t just a virtue, it’s a necessity. You might feel like you’ve finally got an agreement, only to watch it unravel the next day. Progress? It’s measured in inches, not miles.
Let’s talk about one of those early projects. Picture this: you’re setting up a joint venture with a local factory. The building’s seen better days, the machines are outdated, and the workers? They’re just not sure about all this. At first, there’s a lot of resistance—why change something that’s “good enough”? But then, you spend real time on the shop floor, listening to their concerns, offering practical fixes. Slowly, things start to shift. Maybe a technician—skeptical at first—gives a new method a try. Maybe a supervisor, who used to keep his distance, starts sharing ideas to help the place run smoother. Bit by bit, trust grows.
But for every step forward, there’s a new obstacle waiting. Supplies are tough to get, and even the simplest materials have to wind their way through a maze of approvals. Because of international sanctions, importing new equipment becomes a logistical nightmare. Imagine waiting weeks for a shipment, only to find out one tiny stamp is missing from a form. Or seeing a deal collapse overnight when government policy shifts.
Yet, it’s not all frustration. There are moments of real ingenuity. When a key machine breaks down and there’s no way to get spare parts, the local team doesn’t give up—they improvise, piecing together a fix from salvaged parts. Or when power cuts threaten production, workers reorganize their shifts to match the electricity schedule, squeezing every productive minute out of the day. These small victories are hard-fought, but they show just how determined everyone is to succeed.
Then there’s the cultural side of things. Meetings aren’t always straightforward. Disagreements rarely come out in the open. Instead, concerns are hinted at, or brought up quietly, one-on-one, after the fact. So, a foreign manager learns to read more than just words—they start picking up on body language, on when a “yes” really means “maybe,” or when someone’s silence is actually a red flag. There are plenty of misunderstandings along the way, but over time, both sides learn how to meet halfway.
I remember one afternoon, a local partner invited the whole foreign team out for a picnic by the river. There was food, music, even a few games. For just a few hours, the stress of work faded away, replaced by laughter and real connection. It was a powerful reminder that, wherever you are, people want the same things: respect, opportunity, and the chance to build something that matters.
Running a business in North Korea? It’s never simple. The challenges are relentless, and the risks are real. But if you’re willing to adapt, to listen, and to keep learning, you really can make a difference—not just on the balance sheet, but in people’s lives too. In the end, it’s a lesson in humility, patience, and the quiet strength of persistence.
